# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 89 (Bu-Vb Pc89)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 89 (*Nisīdana*) concerns the regulation and prescribed measurements of a Buddhist monastic's sitting mat or sitting cloth (*nisīdana*) [SuttaCentral; Hüsken 1997]. The rule stipulates that a monk who makes an oversized sitting cloth must cut it down to the allowable size and confess a *pācittiya* offense [SuttaCentral; Vinayamukha 1983]. The Vibhaṅga explanation specifies that a proper sitting cloth must have a border or fringe (*nisīdanam nāma sadasaṁ vuccati*; cf. *Samantapāsādikā* 777,10), with the rule framed as having been laid down at Sāvatthi [Vinayamukha 1983; Hüsken 1997].
This rule features prominently in canonical and historical accounts of the Second Buddhist Council at Vesālī, where the ninth of the ten contested practices of the Vajjiputtaka monks—using a borderless rug (*adasakaṁ nisīdanam*)—was judged contrary to Dhamma and Vinaya on the authority of Pācittiya 89 [Bapat 1956; Sarao and Long 2017; Vinayamukha 1983; Hüsken 1997]. This historical dispute connects the text to its canonical parallel in the *Sattasatikakkhandhaka* (Kd 22) [SuttaCentral].
Parallels to Pācittiya 89 are attested across all surviving Vinaya traditions, including the Bhikkhupātimokkha and Parivāra in Pali, as well as the Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅgas and Prātimokṣas of the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka, Mahāsāṅghika, and Kāśyapīya traditions preserved in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan [SuttaCentral]. While the rule is widely shared, the numbering and arrangement differ slightly in texts such as the *Upāliparipṛcchāsūtra* [Stache-Rosen 1984]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus reflects extensive shared formulary phrasing with adjacent Vibhaṅga rules concerning personal requisites and cloth articles—most notably Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiyas 90 and 91, Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 22, and several Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules—in addition to cross-language alignments with Tibetan Vinayavibhaṅga and Prātimokṣa texts [DharmaNexus].
